name: ArtifactsBench
description: ArtifactsBench is a benchmark and automated, multimodal evaluation paradigm for visual code generation. It comprises 1,825 diverse executable queries across nine primary domains (Game Development, SVG Generation, Web Applications, Simulations, Data Science, Management Systems, Multimedia Editing, Quick Tools, and Others), stratified into Easy/Medium/Hard tiers. The framework renders each artifact and captures its dynamic behavior via temporal (three-step) screenshots, which alongside the source code are assessed by a Multimodal LLM (MLLM)-as-Judge guided by fine-grained, per-task checklists. It evaluates over 30 leading LLMs and achieves 94.4% ranking consistency with WebDev Arena and up to 90.95% pairwise agreement with human experts.
creator: Tencent Hunyuan Team
citeAs: Tencent Hunyuan Team. ArtifactsBench: Bridging the Visual-Interactive Gap in LLM Code Generation Evaluation. arXiv:2507.04952v2 [cs.CL], 2025.
rai:dataCollection: Tasks were aggregated from expert showcases, open SVG/web-snippet datasets, web case studies, and LLM visual-to-query generation from screenshots. Automated filters dropped incomplete, non-visual, license-violating, duplicate, trivial, or non-interactive items, prioritizing dynamics (state changes, animations, responsiveness). The curated pool seeded further expansion via LLM generation and refinement. Experts rewrote prompts for clarity, completeness, and executability; LLM rewriting added diverse styles; humans verified. A multi-stage pipeline combining expert sourcing with LLM generation and refinement was used.
rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping, Software Collection, Secondary Data analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Expert showcases, open SVG/web-snippet datasets, web case studies, and LLM visual-to-query generation from screenshots.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Two-stage de-duplication and contamination control: (i) MinHash plus semantic similarity over prompts, checklists, and normalized DOM/CSS/JS; (ii) screenshot perceptual hashing to catch visually near-identical artifacts. Flagged items were re-authored or discarded. Difficulty was assigned post hoc by aggregated performance of 30+ models to enforce a 30%/40%/30% Easy/Medium/Hard split (realized as 559/611/655). Sub-categories were tagged by a lightweight classifier with human spot-checks. Tasks solved only by brittle hacks were revised or removed.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Automated filters dropped incomplete, non-visual, license-violating, duplicate, trivial, or non-interactive items. Two-stage de-duplication: MinHash + semantic similarity over prompts, checklists, and normalized DOM/CSS/JS; screenshot perceptual hashing to catch visually near-identical artifacts. Experts rewrote prompts for clarity, completeness, and executability. Solvability validation collected candidate solutions from multiple model families and pruned underspecified items. Execution was standardized with headless Chromium (Playwright) at 1024x768 resolution with deterministic seeds.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each query was paired with a 10-dimension checklist covering visual, interactional, and code qualities. Checklists were LLM-drafted (using Hunyuan-Turbos) and then human-refined for specificity and screenability. A 10% manually curated seed anchored calibration and achieved Cohen's kappa >= 0.8 among annotators; the seed was reused as few-shot references. The 10 items were grouped into five vision-oriented and five code-oriented dimensions. For human validation, 280 queries with corresponding data from 6 models were independently scored by multiple engineers with extensive front-end development experience following a double-blind protocol; annotators remained unaware of the MLLM's scores and samples appeared in randomized order. The final human ground-truth score represents the median of individual annotators' ratings.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Inter-annotator agreement was measured using Cohen's kappa, achieving kappa >= 0.8 among annotators on the 10% manually curated seed. Pairwise consistency rate (Pair ACC) was used to quantify agreement between the automated MLLM referee and human experts, measuring the proportion of concordant pairwise rankings out of all unique pairs. The automated evaluation achieved up to 90.95% pairwise agreement with human experts (Gemini-2.5-Pro with multiple screenshots). Cross-judge robustness was assessed by comparing rankings from Gemini-2.5-Pro and Qwen2.5-VL-72B, showing highly consistent partial-order constraints.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 10 checklist dimensions per query; multiple human annotators per item in the 280-instance validation study (median of individual ratings used as ground truth)
rai:annotatorDemographics: Multiple engineers with extensive front-end development experience; specific demographic details not reported.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Hunyuan-Turbos (checklist generation), Gemini-2.5-Pro (MLLM-as-Judge referee, query classification), Qwen2.5-VL-72B (MLLM-as-Judge referee), Playwright/headless Chromium (artifact execution and screenshot capture), lightweight classifier (sub-category tagging)
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The benchmark, evaluation harness, and baseline results are open-sourced at https://artifactsbenchmark.github.io. Dataset specs, checklist templates, evaluation scripts, and referee settings are released. Future work targets richer dynamics beyond discrete screenshots, agentic multi-turn self-debugging, and broader artifact domains. Specific versioning, update frequency, and deprecation policies are not explicitly stated.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset explicitly filters out queries involving sensitive personal information (e.g., phone numbers, addresses, or other identifiable details) as part of the quality filtering process.
rai:dataSocialImpact: ArtifactsBench provides the community with a scalable and accurate tool to accelerate the development of user-centric generative models. By enabling holistic, automated, and reproducible evaluation of interactive visual artifacts, it aims to advance LLM capabilities in generating high-fidelity, functional interactive visual artifacts that are central to user experience in modern applications.
rai:dataBiases: The benchmark is self-constructed, which may introduce selection bias in task coverage. Tasks are sourced from expert showcases, open datasets, and LLM-generated content, which may not fully represent all real-world use cases. The difficulty calibration is based on aggregated performance of 30+ LLMs, which may reflect biases in the evaluated model families.
rai:dataLimitations: The current methodology evaluates dynamic behavior by capturing screenshots at fixed intervals, which may not fully capture the fluidity, correctness, and robustness of highly complex, long-horizon, or state-dependent interactions. The benchmark focuses on single-turn artifact generation and does not assess agentic or iterative development capabilities. MLLM referees can suffer from hallucination, prompt sensitivity, limited awareness of engineering/code quality, and version drift. Minor discrepancies between referees are observed in fine-grained scoring of complex interactive tasks, reflecting potential cognitive biases in how different MLLMs interpret long-horizon interaction logic and dynamic visual feedback.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of LLMs on interactive visual code generation tasks. The benchmark supports fine-grained capability analysis across nine domains and three difficulty tiers. It is intended for benchmarking and ranking LLMs, providing diagnostic insights on strengths and failure modes, and validating automated evaluation pipelines against human preferences.
